fixes.explanation: That's the one, baker. The psalm says it plain: "Sing the glory of His name; make His praise glorious." The whole earth is in the choir, and God's name is the song. That's what the singing is for.
Gathering sounds like a plan, friend. A meeting, a whiteboard, maybe a name tag. But the psalm says God's power is so great that His enemies "…cower before You." Cowering is what the verse gives us.

Dry land, friend. The psalm says, "He turned the sea into dry land; they passed through the waters on foot…" People crossing a sea on foot. I can't even hop across my own bakery without wondering if my gold base is going to catch a crumb.

That's a different story, baker. Water turning to blood is in Exodus 7:20, and this psalm doesn't say that about the sea. It says, "He turned the sea into dry land; they passed through the waters on foot…" (Ps 66:6). The sea became dry land.

True, and I love this part. The psalm says, "He turned the sea into dry land; they passed through the waters on foot; there we rejoiced in Him." The people are rejoicing in God there. That line is worth singing.
I get why you'd pause, friend. But it's right there in the verse: "they passed through the waters on foot; there we rejoiced in Him." The psalm says they rejoiced there, so the statement is true.

Humble sounds nice, and I'd love to see it, friend. But the verse says, "Do not let the rebellious exalt themselves." The psalm names exalting themselves as the thing not to let happen. And it comes right after saying God rules forever by His power.
True. The psalm says, "I cried out to Him with my mouth and praised Him with my tongue." Crying out and praising sit side by side in the same verse. The psalmist puts them together.

I see why you'd pause, friend, since those feel like two different moods. But the psalm puts them together: "I cried out to Him with my mouth and praised Him with my tongue." Both are in the same verse, so the statement is true.
